findings.title: MDH did not provide adequate guidance and oversight regarding 304 interagency agreements valued at $329.5 million that MDH administrations entered into with units of State universities.
findings.description: MDH lacked a formal methodology to determine if interagency agreements were cost-beneficial compared to other options like competitive procurement or budgeted positions. Services provided through these agreements often augmented staff beyond budgeted positions and did not always align with the university's mission, while administrative fees appeared excessive.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH provide oversight of and guidance to its administrations regarding agreements with State institutions of higher education; evaluate existing interagency agreements to determine whether each arrangement is appropriate and the most cost beneficial option for MDH; refrain from executing agreements to augment its staff; establish procedures to perform a documented analysis to determine the most cost beneficial option for MDH to obtain services prior to entering into future interagency agreements; and ensure that the administrative fees are reasonable when it is determined appropriate to use an interagency agreement.

findings.title: MDH did not establish procedures to help ensure the agencies responsible for administering interagency agreements verified that the appropriate services were provided by the universities at the agreed-upon costs.
findings.description: MDH lacked procedures to verify that services were provided at agreed-upon costs. PHPA-IDB did not adequately monitor individuals, work assignments remained incomplete, individual evaluations were delayed and lacked detail, and billing rates were not verified against contracts or supported by approved timesheets for some charges totaling $12,067.

dollar_amounts.context: salaries paid for this agreement as of August 1, 2016

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH establish procedures to help ensure the agencies responsible for administering interagency agreements verify that the appropriate services were provided by the universities at the agreed-upon costs; ensure that PHPA-IDB immediately develops work assignments for each individual provided under the aforementioned agreement; ensure that PHPA-IDB performs evaluations of individuals twice annually, and ensure that these evaluations are sufficiently detailed; and as part of the invoice approval process, ensure that PHPA-IDB verifies rates billed to the individual contracts, and obtains and reviews approved timesheets for each individual invoiced.

findings.title: MDH did not always comply with State procurement requirements regarding the award of sole source and emergency contracts.
findings.description: MDH awarded sole source and emergency contracts totaling approximately $45.4 million without adequate justification or price negotiations. Specific instances included unjustified sole source awards for psychiatric and physician services, higher labor rates than competitive procurements, and an emergency procurement with inaccurate information provided to the Board of Public Works.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH ensure sufficient justifications exist for sole source and emergency procurements, and that those justifications are documented; ensure sole source and emergency contract awards provide the most favorable prices, and conduct documented price negotiations as appropriate; ensure that the vendor selection process is handled appropriately; and provide accurate information to the BPW and notify the BPW of the aforementioned erroneous statement.

findings.title: MDH did not have a formal monitoring procedure to ensure that it consistently complied with publication requirements for service and information technology contract awards.
findings.description: MDH lacked a formal monitoring procedure to ensure contract awards were published on eMaryland Marketplace within 30 days as required. Testing of 17 contracts totaling $164.3 million disclosed that 8 contract awards totaling $90 million were not published timely, with seven remaining unpublished as of April 2017.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH establish a formal monitoring procedure to ensure that all applicable contract awards are published on eMM not more than 30 days after the execution and approval of the contract as required.

findings.title: MDH did not always comply with State procurement regulations with respect to bidding requirements and retention of critical procurement documentation. Additionally, MDH also awarded a contract for an amount substantially higher than could be supported by the related bid.
findings.description: MDH lacked procedures to record and secure bids upon receipt, failed to retain critical procurement documentation including financial proposals for contracts totaling $34.4 million, and awarded a pharmaceutical services contract for approximately $5.1 million which was substantially higher than the single vendor bid of $1.9 million without justification.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH establish procedures to record vendor bids upon receipt and to secure vendor bids prior to opening; ensure that at least two employees witness the bid openings, and maintain documentation of the employees present; maintain complete procurement documentation, including all bidder financial and technical proposals; ensure contract award amounts are consistent with bid documents or that adequate justification is maintained to support contract award amounts that differ from the supporting bids; and in the future, when significant changes are made to the scope of services or goods being procured, either amend the published solicitation or provide a written justification for why an amendment is not needed.

findings.title: OIG had not audited certain private providers for more than five years and did not always conduct private provider audits in a comprehensive manner.
findings.description: As of June 1, 2016, 22 private providers had not been audited for more than five years. OIG significantly reduced the scope of work for 50 providers with reported grant expenditures totaling $329.4 million by performing only desk audits, which are less effective in determining cost allowability and identifying control weaknesses.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH ensure that OIG completes its grant audits on a timely basis; and future audits are performed in a comprehensive manner.

findings.title: OIG did not have a formal process for oversight and monitoring to ensure corrective actions were taken by both local health departments and private providers.
findings.description: OIG lacked a formal written policy for oversight and monitoring of corrective actions. Review of 10 LHD audit reports with grant awards totaling $1.2 billion disclosed 69 findings, and follow-up on prior audit findings in 8 reports found that 41 percent were repeated.

dollar_amounts.context: grant awards totaling in 10 LHD audit reports that were issued between June 2014 and May 2016

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH ensure that the OIG establishes a formal process to actively monitor corrective actions taken to address its audit findings.

findings.title: Sensitive personally identifiable information within a database and data file was stored without adequate safeguards.
findings.description: Sensitive personally identifiable information including social security numbers was stored in clear text. One NEDSS database table contained 91,252 unique social security numbers and one HMIS data file contained 123,832 unique social security numbers as of early fiscal year 2017.
findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH properly protect sensitive PII information by encryption or other substantial mitigating controls.

findings.title: Network access to critical MDH internal network devices was not properly restricted, intrusion detection prevention system coverage was not complete or adequate, and certain wireless connections were not configured securely.
findings.description: Firewall rules allowed unnecessary network level access to critical devices. Unused firewall rules representing a security risk existed for 217 rules. IDPS was set to log rather than block traffic and did not cover encrypted traffic. Four wireless connections used insecure encryption protocols.
findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH configure its firewalls to properly protect all critical network devices; perform and document periodic reviews of its firewalls' rule bases to ensure that only necessary rules remain active and unnecessary rules are deleted/disabled based on these reviews; configure its network-based IDPS devices to prevent high-risk malicious traffic from entering the network and to continuously log lower-risk malicious traffic for review and possible investigation; perform a documented review and assessment of its network security risks and identify how IDPS and/or HIPS coverage should be best applied to its network and implement this coverage for traffic (including encrypted traffic) from all untrusted parties; and use the strongest possible encryption method available to protect data in transit over MDH wireless connections.

findings.title: Malware protection for MDH computers was not sufficient to provide the Office of Information Technology with adequate assurance that these computers were properly protected.
findings.description: OIT did not verify malware protection software was operational on all supported computers. Outdated versions of malware protection software were running on 1,828 computers as of January 2017. OIT lacked assurance for approximately 8,200 computers without OIT support and identified workstations with unauthorized administrative rights.
findings.recommendation: We recommend that OIT ensure that all MDH computers are running current versions of the malware protection software and that malware signatures provided by the malware protection software vendor are installed on these computers immediately upon issuance, document these efforts, and retain the documentation for future reference; that commonly vulnerable applications on MDH workstations and servers were frequently updated; and that administrative rights on all MDH workstations and servers are restricted to only system/network administrators or non–IT personnel authorized in writing to have such rights, with documentation supporting these authorizations retained for future reference.

findings.title: Information technology contractors had unnecessary network-level access to the MDH network.
findings.description: IT contractors working on-site at MDH locations had unnecessary network-level access because their traffic was not filtered. OIT lacked a centralized schedule of all IT contractors working onsite and was unaware of the extent of this access.
findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH limit IT contractors' network-level access to only those network devices and ports required for them to perform their duties; and create and maintain, on a current basis, a centralized schedule of all IT contractor personnel working onsite within MDH and use this schedule to ensure that network-level access for these contractors is appropriately limited as noted in the aforementioned recommendation.

findings.title: Controls were not established to ensure collections were properly accounted for, deposited, and secured.
findings.description: MDH lacked adequate controls over cash receipts. Verification of deposits was not independent, segregation of duties between cash receipts and accounts receivable was inadequate, access to mail containing checks was not restricted, and remotely deposited checks totaling approximately $33.1 million were not destroyed in a timely manner as of May 9, 2016.

dollar_amounts.context: collections processed by DGA via mail or walk-in from other MDH units receiving support services totaled approximately in fiscal year 2015
collections processed by DGA were posted to accounts receivable records in fiscal year 2015

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH comply with the Accounting Procedures Manual and the Policy on the Use of Remote Deposit Services. Specifically, we recommend that MDH ensure that the deposit verification is performed by an employee who does not handle or record collections; collections are verified to deposit using the related initial record; proper segregation of duties are established over cash receipts and accounts receivable functions; access to mail is adequately restricted to authorized personnel only; and remotely deposited checks are destroyed in a timely manner and independently reconciled to the initial check logs.

findings.title: Overtime earned by certain Secure Evaluation and Therapeutic Treatment Program employees for an extended period appeared questionable and was not investigated.
findings.description: Review of overtime disclosed excessive overtime for 12 employees that had not been investigated. Overtime payments of approximately $2.7 million exceeded budgeted amounts by approximately $2.2 million, or 506 percent, between fiscal years 2013 and 2016.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH investigate the legitimacy of the overtime for the employees cited as having questionable overtime; and take necessary actions to reduce overtime, consistent with budgetary levels, and ensure that overtime charges are charged against proper agency budgets.

findings.title: MDH did not comply with certain corporate purchasing card requirements relating to the sharing of cards and certain purchasing activities.
findings.description: Testing of 61 transactions disclosed instances where corporate purchasing cards were shared (13 transactions totaling $14,200), purchases were split to avoid limits ($44,250), and gift cards were purchased ($6,500) in violation of policy. Expenditures totaled approximately $25.3 million during fiscal year 2015.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH comply with the Corporate Purchasing Card Policy and Procedures Manual. Specifically, we recommend that MDH ensure that purchasing cards are not shared by more than one employee so that individual accountability exists for each purchase; purchasing card purchases are not artificially split into smaller purchases to circumvent the procurement regulations and individual transaction limits; and purchasing cards are not used to purchase gift cards.

findings.title: MDH physical inventory procedures did not comply with certain Department of General Services requirements.
findings.description: MDH's physical inventory procedures were not in compliance with DGS Inventory Control Manual. For one unit, missing equipment valued at $910,000 had not been investigated or reported to DGS as required. Physical inventories of sensitive equipment for 6 units totaling $17.3 million were not completed annually.

findings.recommendation: We recommend that MDH comply with the requirements of the Department of General Services' Inventory Control Manual. Specifically, we recommend that MDH investigate and resolve missing items identified through physical inventories; report missing or stolen items to DGS within 10 days of discovery; and conduct annual physical inventories of sensitive equipment.

extraction.agency_response_summary: The Department of Health concurred with all recommendations for Finding 1. MDH has provided oversight and guidance to its administrations regarding interagency agreements, removed authority of offices to use IAs without Secretary approval, implemented policies prohibiting hiring new staff by new IAs, analyzes IA alternatives, and implemented standard rates for administrative fees.
